query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Trace Y doping in AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ high-entropy alloy bond coats will enhance coating durability by promoting the formation of an adherent, stable α-Al₂O₃ scale and by reducing excessive grain growth under high-temperature corrosive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ eutectic high-entropy alloy bond coat prepared by laser cladding (undoped).
generation.intervention: Incorporate a trace level (approximately 0.5 atomic percent) of yttrium into the feedstock prior to laser cladding.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 900 °C for 60 hours under hot corrosion conditions (75% Na₂SO₄ + 25% NaCl molten salt environment).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced formation of a uniform and adherent α-Al₂O₃ thermally grown oxide and a modestly refined grain structure.
generation.mechanism: Y atoms segregate to grain boundaries and the coating surface, acting as reactive sites that promote the nucleation and adherence of an α-Al₂O₃ scale while retarding grain boundary mobility to reduce undesirable grain growth.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, the Y-doped coating will exhibit approximately 10–15% lower grain growth and at least a 50% reduction in the spallation area during high-temperature corrosion tests.
generation.baseline: Coating without Y doping under identical processing and exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to be maintained up to about 900 °C in environments similar to the molten salt hot-corrosion test; performance outside this regime or at significantly higher temperatures is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal doping concentration and potential trade-offs with other properties (e.g., mechanical integrity) require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ bond coats via laser cladding: one with approximately 0.5 at% Y doping and one undoped. Subject both sets to heat treatment at 900 °C for 60 hours in a molten salt (75% Na₂SO₄ + 25% NaCl) bath. Characterize surface oxide scale morphology, measure grain size via EBSD, and assess spallation area percentage via imaging.
measurements: Grain size evolution (percentage increase) compared to as-deposited state.
Spallation area quantified as a percentage of the total surface area.
Adhesion and uniformity of the thermally grown oxide scale (via microscopy).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped coatings do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., less than 10–15% lower grain growth and less than 50% reduction in spallation area) relative to the undoped samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, the Y and Hf co-doping did not change the microstructure morphology and phase structure of the coatings but did improve the thermal stability and resistance of the hot corrosion oxide scale spallation, providing a certain amount of data and theoretical support for the application of EHEA coatings as high

The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. 1. The YHf co-doping did not alter the solidification microstructure and phase structure of the EHEA coating. The microstructure morphologies of the top and bottom portions of coatings were composed of cellular and columnar dendrites, respectively. And the phase structure consisted of FCC and BCC/B2. 2. After heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h, the BCC/B2 structure was relatively stable in all coatings while the nanoscale Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC. 3. papers.title: Thermal Stability and Hot Corrosion Performance of the AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ High-Entropy Alloy Coating by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ eutectic high-entropy alloy coatings (both undoped and Y/Hf co-doped variants)
papers.approach: Laser cladding to prepare coatings with and without co-doping of reactive elements (Y and Hf); subsequent heat treatment at 900 °C and hot corrosion tests in molten salts.
papers.findings: The Y and Hf co-doped coatings exhibited reduced grain growth (15.7% increase vs. 27.5% in undoped) and a lower spallation area (5.67% vs. 14.98%) after hot corrosion, indicating improved thermal stability and oxidation resistance.
papers.mechanism: The reactive elements (Y and Hf) are proposed to enhance the sluggish diffusion intrinsic to HEAs and improve the adhesion of the hot corrosion oxide scale, thereby inhibiting spallation.

papers.title: Preparation of VZrHfNbTa High-Entropy Alloy-Based High-Temperature Oxidation-Resistant Coating and Its Bonding Mechanism.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloy-based coatings (VZrHfNbTa) on substrates
papers.approach: Hot-press sintering to form Hf-rich surface coatings with interfacial diffusion of zirconium, resulting in a gradient HfZr alloy layer between the coating and substrate.
papers.findings: The diffusion of Zr (~60 μm) formed a gradient composite layer that enhanced the adhesion between the coating and the substrate, significantly improving the oxidation resistance compared to uncoated samples.
papers.mechanism: The gradient layer, formed by the interaction of Hf (provided via coating) and diffusing Zr from the substrate, improves bond coat durability by enhancing interfacial bonding and providing a barrier to elemental intermixing during high-temperature exposure.

papers.title: Refractory Metal Intermetallic Composites, High-Entropy Alloys, and Complex Concentrated Alloys: A Route to Selecting Substrate Alloys and Bond Coat A
papers.system: Various high-entropy and complex concentrated alloys used as bond coat systems in ultra-high-temperature materials
papers.approach: Mapping alloy design parameters (δ, Δχ, VEC) to select substrate and bond coat alloy compositions that favor the formation of protective αAl₂O₃ scales.
papers.findings: It was identified that bond coats designed with proper alloying can form an adherent, stable αAl₂O₃ thermally grown oxide, which is crucial for durability in high-temperature environments.
papers.mechanism: Selected compositional windows promote the formation of αAl₂O₃, which acts as a protective barrier against oxidation and CMAS attack, ensuring coating reliability over time.

established: Reactive element (e.g., Y and Hf) doping in high-entropy alloy coatings can improve thermal stability and oxidation resistance.

directions.direction: Reactive element doping with a single element (Y) to promote scale adhesion and reduce grain growth.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the degradation mechanism (spallation and oxidation) by enhancing α‐Al₂O₃ scale formation and stabilizing the microstructure. Physics and prior evidence from Y and Hf co‐doping studies support that reactive elements improve high‐temperature performance. The approach is feasible via feedstock modifications.

directions.direction: Reactive element doping with a single element (Hf) to pin grain boundaries and modify oxidation behavior.
directions.assessment: This intervention relies on the known benefits of Hf in reducing grain growth and enhancing oxide scale adhesion (via formation of HfO₂ or Hf-rich particles). It directly addresses durability under high-temperature and corrosive environments and is supported by studies where Hf improved oxidation resistance.

directions.direction: Incorporation of oxide-dispersion particles (Y₂O₃ nanoparticles) within the bond coat.
directions.assessment: Adding a minute fraction of Y₂O₃ aims to refine the microstructure and act as an oxygen scavenger, thereby improving the formation of a uniform, adherent oxide scale. Prior work on Y₂O₃-dispersed coatings supports grain refinement and oxidation resistance; the physics of heterogeneous nucleation and dispersion strengthening are well established.

directions.direction: Optimization of laser cladding process parameters to create a refined, uniform, and strongly bonded microstructure.
directions.assessment: Adjusting process variables (e.g., laser power, scan speed) can improve the microstructure (refined eutectic structure with reduced porosity) and metallurgical bonding. This intervention directly lowers defect densities and residual stresses that compromise durability. The approach is supported by studies linking processing parameters to coating microstructure and performance.
